prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a single, nameable invention with a clear mechanism: trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels on the clock transition, which combines the statistics of many atoms with Lamb-Dicke confinement. The result is the most accurate measurement made by any method, at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, confirmed by independent laboratories on several continents and compared across fibre links. It opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre level and a redefinition of the second. It is also the one candidate on which all eight opening ballots agree on both ranking and the two-name credit, and seven of eight members place it in the top six. That convergence is not itself merit, but the independent assessments of originality, attribution and maturity point the same way, and the credit is unusually compact: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the performance frontier.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: Hall and Hansch (2005) for the frequency comb and Wineland (2012) for single-ion control cover adjacent ground, and Ye's comb work belongs partly to that lineage. A second concern is that the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the application milestone is still ahead, and several groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, single-ion clocks) contributed demonstrations that two names do not represent. I think the first concern is answered by the distinct magic-wavelength concept and by the fact that the lattice clock is a different physical architecture, and the second is an application milestone, not a doubt about the science, but a committee member could reasonably weigh them more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B014) first as a clear discovery of nature that opened a new window, with Halzen and Karle as a compact credit, while ranking optical lattice clocks fourth.
responses.response: I agree that B014 is a real discovery and that the diffuse flux is confirmed. My difficulty is attribution and maturity of the part that makes it a Nobel-level story. Several members, including you, note that two names stand in for a very large collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, and that independent detector confirmation is still limited. The lattice clock has none of these problems: it is an invention by named groups with many independent replications at the 1e-18 level. I would not call it a stronger window on nature than neutrino astronomy, but I judge it the more securely attributed and more clearly confirmed. If the committee prefers a discovery-of-nature prize, B014 is a serious candidate, and I would not oppose it as an alternative; I just do not rank it above B015 on the evidence in these ballots.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems (B005) first as the strongest fundamental-theory candidate, and notes that Hall and Hansch were recognised in 2005 for frequency combs on which the clocks build.
responses.response: I take the 2005 overlap seriously, and I raise it against my own first choice. But the comb is a ruler for optical frequencies, while the lattice clock is a separate scheme for the atomic reference, whose key idea is the magic wavelength; Katori's contribution does not follow from the comb prize. On B005 I accept that the Jarzynski and Crooks relations are elegant and well tested, but only you rank it, and your own attribution note says Evans, Gallavotti and Cohen leave the credit incomplete. That makes the claim narrower than the lattice clocks, whose credit you describe as clean and uncontested. I would like to hear what quantitative experimental consequence the committee would put in a citation beyond single-molecule pulling work.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B039) first as an original platform with very large impact on quantum information, while stating that he is close to the field, and ranks trapped ions second.
responses.response: I take your point about impact, and I ranked B039 fourth myself. My reservation is the one you and I both note: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits touches the same field, and the credit omits Devoret, Girvin and Huang, who may be at least as essential as the proposal-plus-experiment core. Because you flag your own closeness, I would like the discussion to test whether B039 is a distinct discovery rather than a continuation of the 2025 recognition. I would hold it back for a later year, and I am more comfortable with B009 as the quantum-information alternative, since the Cirac-Zoller proposal and Blatt's experiments are cleanly separable from the 2012 prize in the ballots.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators (B018) first as a long-standing omission with two decades of confirmation, and ranks optical lattice clocks second.
responses.response: We agree on lattice clocks, and I respect your case for topological insulators, which is probably the most influential condensed-matter concept in the pool. The difficulty is the credit, which every ballot that ranks it flags as contestable: Mele is a co-author of the Z2 paper, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation, and the three-name limit forces a choice that members resolve in different ways (B018 versus B003 with Xue). A prize whose names the committee cannot defend is a weaker prize than one with a clean two-name credit. If the committee can settle the credit, I would not object to B018 as a serious candidate, but at present I rank it below B015 for that reason, not for lack of merit.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, citing magic-wavelength confinement, independent confirmation at 1e-18 and a fair two-person credit, and sees twisted bilayer graphene as slightly early.
responses.response: I agree on B015 and on the credit, and I would add one point to your maturity argument: international comparisons between laboratories, not only agreement within each, make the 1e-18 claim robust. On B030 I think your concern that recognition may be slightly early is reasonable, since the superconductivity mechanism is still debated, and the fact that Cao is outside the credit adds to the attribution difficulty. I would not support a two-part prize pairing the clocks with it at this stage, since the union of names cannot exceed three people and the pairing would require dropping one of the clock laureates.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as already covering the surrounding ground.
Whether two names fairly represent the lattice clock field given the contributions of other groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, single-ion clocks), which the supplied credit does not include.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as confirmation of maturity or as a reason to wait for it.
Whether a two-part prize with a second achievement would be worth giving up one of the clock laureates, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connection to report: Jun Ye is associated with John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, where I spent a research stay during my doctoral period; I regard it as background, not a personal relationship with Ye, but the committee may wish to note it. I have also had general European quantum-memory and quantum-optics contacts in the atomic-physics community, and a WACQT programme-management role, which touches B039 (superconducting circuits) and neighbouring quantum-information candidates (B009, B032) as a field, without any documented specific relationship to the credited individuals. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
